meta.description: War and economy indicators for U.S. midterm elections 1946-2022 plus 2026 current values; every number sourced; null = not found / not yet collected.

conventions.term_to_date: calendar years from the start of the president's current four-year term through the election year
conventions.house_vote: percent of all votes cast (not two-party)

rdi_pc.basis: annual 1946 vs 1945 (quarterly series A229RX0Q048SBEA begins 1947Q1, so no Q3 1946 value)

unemp_oct.basis: ANNUAL AVERAGE 1946 (no monthly October figure: UNRATE begins Jan 1948); persons 14 years and over (pre-1947 definition); 1945 annual = 1.9
unemp_oct.series: BLS CPS annual averages, Table 1 (2009 edition)

house_vote.source_note: Percent of ALL House votes (not two-party), Brookings Vital Statistics on Congress Table 2-2 'Popular Vote and House Seats Won by Party, 1946-2024' (excludes districts with unopposed candidates where no vote was recorded).

house_vote_prev.source_note: Wikipedia infobox/summary table (Brookings Table 2-2 starts in 1946, so 1944 is not on the Brookings basis).

models.name: Hibbs 'Bread and Peace' model (presidential elections)
models.finding: Incumbent party's two-party presidential vote depends on only two things: (1) weighted-average growth of real disposable personal income per capita over the term (quarterly log changes x400, geometric lag weights over 15 quarters, lambda = 0.914; election-quarter weight cut to 1/3), and (2) cumulative U.S. military fatalities from hostile deployments the incumbent party started (Korea, Vietnam, Iraq), in thousands. 2007 estimates (N=14, 1952-2004): constant 46.2, +3.61 vote points per 1 pt of weighted income growth, -0.307 points per 1,000 fatalities; adjusted R2 = .826, root MSE = 2.42. Per-capita version: -0.050 points per fatality per million population. Fatality inputs: Korea 1952 = 29,260; Vietnam 1968 = 28,896; Vietnam 1972 = 0 (Nixon did not start the war); Iraq 2004 = 1,130 (end of Oct 2004).
models.how_fatalities_enter: Linear penalty on cumulative KIA over the term, counted only for the party that initiated the deployment. Hibbs said fatalities were decisive only in 1952 and 1968, and that roughly 1,500 Afghanistan deaths under Obama (about 5 per million) were 'way too small to have great electoral effect'.
models.track_record: In-sample errors: 1952 -1.30, 1968 +1.37, 1972 +2.52, 1996 +4.76, 2000 -4.49, 2004 -0.84 (1996 and 2000 are the only poorly fit years per Hibbs). Out-of-sample 2004 prediction 52.16% (error -0.92). Mean absolute error 1.49 points over 14 elections. 2012 forecast: Obama 47.2% of the two-party vote (a loss); Obama was re-elected.
models.application_2024_2026: not found (no 2024 or 2026 Bread and Peace forecast found; douglas-hibbs.com returned a fetch error)
models.original_paper: Hibbs, D. A. (2000). Bread and Peace Voting in U.S. Presidential Elections. Public Choice 104(1-2): 149-180.

models.name: Tufte (1975) midterm referendum model
models.finding: Midterm vote loss of the president's party (two-party House vote minus its average over the 8 prior elections) = -11.083 + 0.133 x September Gallup approval + 0.035 x yearly change in real disposable income per capita (dollars). R2 = 0.912, N = 8 midterms (1938-1970, excluding 1942). A 10-point change in approval is associated with 1.3 points of House vote; a $100 change in real income per capita with 3.5 points. Tufte calls the midterm 'a referendum on the performance of the President and his administration's management of the economy'. Its 1974 forecast was 60.8% Democratic vs. 58.9% actual.
models.citation: Tufte, E. R. (1975). Determinants of the Outcomes of Midterm Congressional Elections. American Political Science Review 69(3): 812-826.

models.name: Lewis-Beck & Tien referendum / 'Structure-X' House model
models.finding: House seat change of the president's party = f(June Gallup presidential approval, real disposable income growth over the first two quarters of the election year, midterm dummy). 2018 version: Seats = -44.83 + 0.82 x approval + 4.91 x income growth - 28.53 x midterm; R2 = .59, RMSE = 18.06 seats, N = 35. 2018 structural forecast -30 Republican seats, -44 after averaging with an expert index. 2010 forecast: Republican gain of 22 seats.

models.name: Abramowitz generic-ballot model
models.finding: Seat change of the president's party = f(generic congressional ballot margin, number of seats the party is defending); earlier versions (2010) also used presidential approval and a midterm term. April 2025 version (20 midterms, 1946-2022): each generic-ballot point is worth about 2.6 House seats; each extra seat defended costs about 0.54 seats; explains over 80% of House variance. With a tied generic ballot, it projects about a 13-seat Republican House loss in 2026. Track record: 16 of 20 House predictions within 10 seats; 2022 predicted a Democratic loss of 18 vs. 9 actual; largest misses were 1994 (underestimated Democratic losses by 22) and 2006 (overestimated Republican losses by 17). 2010 forecast: Republican gain of 43.

models.name: Campbell surge-and-decline (revised theory)
models.finding: In presidential years, the winning presidential party gains House seats and votes (the surge); at the next midterm, that boost disappears. Midterm losses are proportional to the party's prior presidential vote margin. In Campbell's 1868-1988 estimates, the typical midterm penalty was over 4 points of House vote and about 44 seats; after accounting for the lost presidential surge, the remainder was about half that size. Campbell's 2010 seats-in-trouble/approval model forecast a Republican gain of 51-52 seats.
models.citation: Campbell, J. E. (1987). The Revised Theory of Surge and Decline. AJPS 31(4): 965-979; Campbell (1991), JOP 53(2): 477-487.

models.name: Other 2010 PS symposium midterm models (for comparison)
models.finding: Bafumi, Erikson & Wlezien (generic ballot, two-step district model) forecast a Republican gain of 51; Cuzan (prior seats, incumbency, midterm, growth and inflation) forecast 27-30. Republicans gained 63 seats (Wikipedia 2010 page also reports 62 in one place).

models.name: Kramer (1971) aggregate economic voting model
models.finding: Economic conditions in the year before an election explain about half of the variance in the congressional vote (1896-1964). Real personal income is the most important factor. Unemployment has no independent effect, and inflation was not significant in the original estimates but showed a role after a data correction (summary by Burdekin, Dallas Fed 1985).
models.citation: Kramer, G. H. (1971). Short-Term Fluctuations in U.S. Voting Behavior, 1896-1964. APSR 65(1): 131-143.

literature.finding: Public support for the Korean and Vietnam wars started high and fell in a logarithmic relationship to cumulative American casualties; specific events had little effect on the trends.
literature.source: Mueller, J. E. (1971). Trends in Popular Support for the Wars in Korea and Vietnam. APSR 65(2): 358-375 (also War, Presidents and Public Opinion, 1973)

literature.finding: In Korea, Vietnam and Iraq, 'as casualties mount, support decreases'. Support for Iraq eroded faster: by early 2005, with about 1,500 combat deaths, a majority called the war a mistake. That was about the share who said so about Vietnam at Tet (1968), when nearly 20,000 Americans had died.
literature.source: Mueller, J. (2005). The Iraq Syndrome. Foreign Affairs 84(6): 44-54

literature.finding: Casualties predict wartime opinion, but Mueller's log-of-cumulative-casualties measure is 'problematic and incomplete'. Marginal (recent) casualties matter, especially when losses are accelerating (Korea and Vietnam data).
literature.source: Gartner, S. S. & Segura, G. M. (1998). War, Casualties, and Public Opinion. Journal of Conflict Resolution 42(3): 278-300

literature.finding: Local losses: California respondents in counties with recently high killed-in-action rates were less likely to support the Vietnam War (about 6,500 respondents in nine polls). The effect was strong through Tet and faded after casualties slowed.
literature.source: Gartner et al., 'All Politics are Local: Local Losses and Individual Attitudes Towards the Vietnam War', JCR (UC Davis release, 1998)

literature.finding: State-level Iraq casualties (dead and wounded per capita) significantly reduced Bush's 2004 vote share relative to 2000. Without the roughly 10,000 U.S. dead and wounded by Election Day, Bush would have won nearly 2% more of the national vote (about 52.3%, 366 electoral votes). Effects were largest in 'blue' states.
literature.source: Karol, D. & Miguel, E. (2007). The Electoral Cost of War: Iraq Casualties and the 2004 U.S. Presidential Election. Journal of Politics 69(3): 633-648

literature.finding: In Republican-held districts, each two Iraq war deaths from the district were associated with about a 1-point Democratic swing (average 2.4 deaths per GOP district). Republicans who voted for the war suffered an extra swing of about 1.6 points. There was no comparable penalty for Democratic incumbents.
literature.source: Grose, C. R. & Oppenheimer, B. I. (2007). The Iraq War, Partisanship, and Candidate Attributes: Variation in Partisan Swing in the 2006 U.S. House Elections. Legislative Studies Quarterly 32(4): 531-557

literature.finding: Republican Senate candidates lost more vote share from 2000 to 2006 where local (state and county) Iraq casualty rates were higher. A two-standard-deviation increase in county casualties cost the Republican incumbent more than 2 points. The authors call this a 'democratic brake on military adventurism, even in small-scale wars'.
literature.source: Kriner, D. L. & Shen, F. X. (2007). Iraq Casualties and the 2006 Senate Elections. Legislative Studies Quarterly 32(4): 507-530, doi:10.3162/036298007782398486

literature.finding: Counter-evidence and conditioning factors: Gelpi, Feaver & Reifler (2005/06) find casualty tolerance depends mainly on beliefs about success. Fox (2009, JCR) finds log war fatalities lowered Democrats' and independents' approval of Bush but not Republicans'. Hill, Herron & Lewis (2010) find no county-level casualty effect in 2008.
literature.source: Literature review by Paul Musgrave summarizing these studies

literature.finding: Hibbs: troop fatalities were decisive only in 1952 (about 29,260 U.S. deaths in Korea at election time) and 1968 (about 28,900 in Vietnam). Voters punish the party that initiated the deployment.
literature.source: Foreign Policy, 'Will U.S. military fatalities sway voters on Election Day?' (Nov 1, 2012)

literature.finding: Midterm House vote responds to presidential approval and to the yearly change in real disposable income per capita (R2 = 0.91, 1938-1970).

Economic fluctuations in the year before an election explain about half of the variance in the congressional vote. Real personal income is the key variable; inflation shows a secondary role after a data correction.
literature.source: Kramer (1971) as summarized in Burdekin, Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Research Paper 8506 (Oct 1985)

literature.finding: Fixed-effects analysis, 1976-2011: a 50-cent quarter-over-quarter rise in gas prices was associated with about a 3.5-point drop in presidential approval (30 cents: about 2 points); a 50-cent higher price level was associated with a 0.75-point drop in consumer sentiment. Simulations implied that a rise to $5 a gallon could cost an incumbent about 2.4 points of vote share. Nate Silver found gas prices add no explanatory power beyond GDP in vote models.
literature.source: John Sides, 'The Political Consequences of Gas Prices', Washington Monthly (Mar 13, 2012)

literature.finding: Random-forest analysis finds a nonlinear link between real gasoline prices and U.S. presidential approval, with out-of-sample predictive value, consistent with a pocketbook mechanism.
literature.source: Gupta, R., Pierdzioch, C. & Tiwari, A. K. (2025). Gasoline Prices and Presidential Approval Ratings of the United States. American Politics Research 53(5): 469-480, doi:10.1177/1532673X251325458

literature.finding: 1974: Wikipedia's 1974 House elections page states that 'This scandal [Watergate], along with high inflation, allowed the Democrats to make large gains' (net +49 seats). Tufte's income-and-approval model predicted 60.8% Democratic vs 58.9% actual.

2022 (AP VoteCast via KFF): half of midterm voters called inflation the single most important factor in their vote, and Republicans did better with them. Four in ten said the Dobbs decision had a major impact on whether they voted; about one in four called it the single most important factor, and about 7 in 10 of those backed Democratic House candidates.

2026 context: the AP-NORC poll (Sept 24-28, 2026) found 65% of adults say higher-than-usual prices are the result of Trump's policies, and 69% say his handling of the cost of living has been worse than expected.

cases.title: Korea: war at the start of the conflict
cases.summary: The Korean War began June 25, 1950, and Wikipedia notes that Truman's popularity 'plummeted for a second time' as it began. Democrats lost a net 28 seats (263 to 235) but kept the House. The economy was strong: real disposable income per capita rose 7.6% (Q3/Q3) and October unemployment was 4.2%. The Democratic share of the all-party House vote fell from 51.6% (1948) to 48.9% (Brookings). A calendar-1950 U.S. hostile-death count was not found.

cases.title: Vietnam escalation plus rising prices
cases.summary: U.S. hostile deaths in Vietnam rose from 1,369 in 1965 to 5,008 in 1966 (Moise). Wikipedia says Johnson's popularity fell 'as the Vietnam War continued to escalate and race riots exploded in cities across the country'; Republicans gained a net 47 seats. Consumer prices were up 3.5% year over year in September (CPI-U), unemployment was 3.7%, and UMich sentiment slipped from 100.0 (Feb) to 91.2 (Aug) and 88.3 (Nov). The Democratic House vote share fell from 56.9% (1964) to 50.5% (Brookings).

cases.title: Watergate plus inflation and recession
cases.summary: Held three months after Nixon's resignation, the election 'occurred in the wake of the Watergate scandal', which 'along with high inflation, allowed the Democrats to make large gains': a net +49 seats, to 291-144. CPI-U was up 11.95% year over year in September, the CPI gasoline index was up 32% from October 1973, real disposable income per capita was down 2.3% (Q3/Q3), and October unemployment was 6.0%. Tufte's model (approval plus real income) predicted a 60.8% Democratic two-party vote; the actual was 58.9%.

cases.title: Deep recession under a new president
cases.summary: Unemployment reached 10.4% in October 1982, and Wikipedia ties Reagan's sinking popularity to 'economic conditions under the 1982 recession'. Democrats gained 26 seats (243 to 269) and won 55.2% of the House vote to 43.4%. Real disposable income per capita was nearly flat (+0.5% Q3/Q3), inflation had cooled to 5.0% (September CPI-U), and gas prices were 5.5% lower than a year earlier.

cases.title: Iraq war midterm
cases.summary: Wikipedia cites the 'sixth-year itch', views of Bush, congressional Republican scandals and 'the handling of the Iraq War and the War in Afghanistan'. Democrats gained 31 seats (to 233) and won 52.3% of the vote to 44.3%. The economy was not a drag: unemployment 4.4%, real disposable income per capita +2.3%, gas prices 18% below a year earlier. The war was costly: DoD counted 822 U.S. deaths in Iraq in 2006 (640 from January to October) plus 65 hostile deaths in Afghanistan. District studies find larger Republican losses where local Iraq casualties were higher (Grose & Oppenheimer; Kriner & Shen).

cases.title: Great Recession aftermath
cases.summary: Unemployment was 9.4% in October 2010, and Wikipedia links Republican gains to 'the continued economic recession' and to the stimulus and health care bills. Republicans won 242 seats (a 63-seat pickup; the page also says 62 in one place). The pre-election models in the PS symposium ranged from +22 (Lewis-Beck & Tien) to +51/52 (Campbell; Bafumi, Erikson & Wlezien). The Afghanistan surge also peaked: 437 U.S. hostile deaths in 2010 (DCAS).

cases.title: Inflation versus Dobbs
cases.summary: CPI-U was up 8.2% year over year in September 2022, gasoline averaged $4.016 in October (+18.6%), and real disposable income per capita was down 3.8% (Q3/Q3), but unemployment was 3.6%. Republicans gained 9 seats (222-213) and won the vote 50.0% to 47.3%; Wikipedia says the 'widely predicted red wave' did not materialize, crediting abortion after Dobbs. In AP VoteCast, half of voters named inflation the top factor and about a quarter named Dobbs, and that quarter backed Democrats about 7 to 3. Abramowitz's generic-ballot model predicted a Democratic loss of 18 seats vs. 9 actual.

gaps: Korean War: U.S. hostile deaths in calendar 1950 (and before the Nov 7, 1950 election) not found; DCAS/CRS give whole-war totals only (33,739 hostile).

Vietnam: hostile-only deaths for 1961-62 not found (NARA all-cause totals used: 16 and 53). Hostile counts for 1965-1970 come from Edwin Moise's Clemson page, which cites no source (each is below the matching NARA all-cause total, as expected). Jan-Oct splits for 1966 and 1970 not found.

Iraq (2006, 2010): calendar-year hostile deaths on the DCAS basis not found. Provided DoD all-cause annual totals (822 in 2006, 60 in 2010) and icasualties Jan-Oct cause-of-death splits (helicopter losses mix hostile and non-hostile).
Operation Inherent Resolve (2014, 2018) and any 2022 hostile deaths by year not found (OIR whole-operation total through Sept 2019: 86 deaths, 17 hostile).
Smaller operations (Lebanon 1958, Lebanon 1982, Libya 1986, Somalia/Haiti 1994): year-specific death counts not found; only whole-operation totals where DCAS lists them.
Gasoline: no October dollar pump price before 1976. 1946-1974 use the CPI gasoline index (CWUR0000SETB01) YoY; 1950, 1954 and 1966 use September readings because October was not published.
Consumer sentiment: no October survey before 1978. 1954-1974 values are the nearest (November) survey, with the last pre-election reading also given; 1946 and 1950 predate the survey.
RDI per capita 1946 is annual (quarterly series begins 1947); unemployment 1946 is the annual average for persons 14+ (UNRATE begins 1948).

House popular vote 1946-2000 uses Brookings Vital Statistics on Congress Table 2-2 (one consistent all-vote series) instead of per-year Wikipedia pages. Wikipedia checks were made only for 1944-1950, and its figures differ slightly (e.g., 1946 D 45.0 vs 44.3; 1948 D 52.6 vs 51.6; 1950 D 49.6 vs 48.9). The fetched text of the 1952 and 1958 Wikipedia pages did not include vote figures. 1944 comes from Wikipedia, so it is not on the Brookings basis.
Hibbs: douglas-hibbs.com returned a fetch error; no 2024 or 2026 Bread and Peace application found.
Gallup ended presidential approval polling at the start of 2026; its last readings (Nov and Dec 2025: 36%) are given with Oct 8, 2026 averages from RCP, NYT and Silver Bulletin.

Iran war: U.S. strike/target counts after April 2026 not found (CENTCOM reported more than 13,000 targets by early April). The latest troop deployment figure found is May 2026 (GlobalSecurity, secondary). The hostile/non-hostile split (11/10) comes from a Fox News live blog citing the Pentagon.
Inflation/gas studies: no specific peer-reviewed study tying inflation to 1978 or 1980 incumbent losses was found; the data are provided (Sept CPI YoY 1978: 8.3%) without a study.

Access note: the FRED .txt URLs given in the brief could not be fetched (permission/provenance block); the equivalent FRED 'Table Data' pages (same series) were used and spot-checked twice for consistency.
September 2026 CPI (due Oct 14) and Q3 2026 GDP/RDI were not yet released as of Oct 11, 2026.
